# The Right to Darkness

There is a place in the high desert where I once stood at midnight and understood, for the first time, that the night sky is not black. It is layered. Above me the Milky Way arched from horizon to horizon like a river of crushed pearl, so dense in places that it seemed less like a collection of stars than a substance, a weather, something you could reach into. Faint patches of light and dark mottled its length. Near the eastern horizon, before the moon rose, there was a soft cone of glow—the zodiacal light, sunlight scattered off dust left behind by comets, hanging in the darkness like a ghost of the day. And beneath everything, so faint you had to trust your peripheral vision to see it, the air itself glowed: a dim green shimmer caused by atoms in the upper atmosphere releasing energy they had borrowed from the sun. Even the emptiest night sky, it turns out, is quietly luminous. Darkness, real darkness, is never nothing.

Under skies like those, observers insist, the Milky Way is bright enough to cast a shadow—your silhouette printed faintly on pale ground by the combined light of a hundred billion suns. I did not test this claim that night. I only stood there feeling something I could not immediately name, and eventually decided it was a kind of grief mixed with recognition: the sense of meeting someone famous whom I had been told about all my life but had never actually seen.

Most people will never have that meeting. By the best recent estimates, more than eighty percent of humanity lives under skies polluted by artificial light, and in North America the figure approaches everyone: roughly four in five people on this continent cannot see the Milky Way from their homes. They live beneath a dome of skyglow, the diffuse amber-white haze that hovers over every city and spreads for miles into the countryside, washing out all but the brightest stars. For them, the Milky Way is not an object of experience but a piece of folklore, like dragons or the hollow earth—a thing known only through pictures. Children grow up, learn in school that our galaxy is a barred spiral containing hundreds of billions of stars, and never once see the faint band of it crossing their own sky. We have erased the largest visible feature of the universe from view and barely paused to notice.

It was not always so. For almost the entire span of human history, night was a country with its own geography, economy, and customs, and everyone was a citizen. Light was expensive. A candle was a purchase, a decision, a small burning coin; poor households made do with rushlights—dried reeds dipped in fat—or went to bed when the sun did, because sitting up cost money. Tallow candles smoked and stank; beeswax was for churches and the rich; whale oil lit the parlors of the wealthy until kerosene democratized lamplight in the nineteenth century. Under these conditions, people organized their lives around whatever free light remained. Farmers harvested by the light of the harvest moon, that full moon nearest the autumn equinox, which rises close to sunset for several nights in a row and hangs low and orange and generous. Anyone who has walked a familiar path under a full moon knows how much can be done in that silver light: enough to bring in the crops, mend a fence, visit a neighbor half a mile down the road.

Sleep itself was different. The historian Roger Ekirch, combing through diaries, court records, medical texts, and literature from the pre-industrial world, documented something startling: for centuries, people in Europe and elsewhere slept in two segments. There was the "first sleep," beginning shortly after dusk, lasting three or four hours; then a period of quiet wakefulness—an hour or more of lying in the dark, sometimes called "the watch"—and then the "second sleep" until morning. This was not insomnia. It was a rhythm, so ordinary that writers rarely bothered to explain it, mentioning first sleep and second sleep the way we mention breakfast and lunch. People used the waking interval to pray, to reflect on their dreams—which felt closer, more visitable, in that drowsy hour—to talk softly with a spouse, to make love, to simply think. Some got up and visited neighbors. The night had a room in it that we have since walled off.

Night was feared, of course. Pre-industrial darkness held real dangers: thieves, wolves, fire, spirits. Towns rang bells and posted watchmen; the very word "curfew" descends from the French *couvre-feu*, "cover fire," the signal to bank your hearth and sleep. But the fear was bounded and shared, a common condition rather than a private anxiety, and against it stood the compensations: the storytelling, the closeness of family around a single flame, the vast theater of the sky performing overhead for anyone who cared to look up. Night was a commons. Everyone held the same deed.

Then we burned the commons down. Gaslight arrived in the early nineteenth century—London demonstrated it on Pall Mall in 1807—and cities discovered they could extend their waking lives into the dark. Paris, bathed in new streetlamps and aglow with intellectual ferment, earned the name City of Light. When Edison's Pearl Street Station began sending electricity through Lower Manhattan in 1882, the transformation accelerated past anything the gaslight era imagined. Night became negotiable. Factories ran shifts. Streets filled at all hours. Within a few generations, the ancient partnership between human activity and the sun dissolved, and staying awake all night stopped being strange and started being a boast. The city that never sleeps wears its insomnia as a crown.

And light became cheap in a way no previous human being could have conceived. Consider the arithmetic: a candle produces roughly thirteen lumens. A single modern LED bulb produces more than a thousand while sipping watts, and a stadium floodlight outshines every candle ever made in colonial Boston combined. We did not merely extend the day; we drowned it. Today the glow of Las Vegas is visible from aircraft a hundred miles away. On the nine-point scale astronomers use to grade sky darkness—from Class 1, pristine wilderness sky, to Class 9, inner-city glare—most urban dwellers live their entire lives at the bottom of the range, where the naked-eye star count collapses from thousands to a few dozen. The stars have not gone anywhere. We have simply built a ceiling between ourselves and them, and forgotten it was there.

The costs are not only aesthetic. Light, deployed carelessly, kills. Sea turtle hatchlings, evolved over a hundred million years to scramble toward the brighter seaward horizon, crawl instead toward beachfront resorts and die on highways. Migrating birds, navigating by stars and moonlight, are drawn into the blaze of cities; by some estimates, collisions with buildings kill hundreds of millions of birds each year in the United States alone, which is why conservation groups now run "Lights Out" campaigns urging cities to dim during migration season. Insects, already in trouble, fare worse: moths that navigated by the moon for millennia spiral helplessly around streetlamps, and studies have shown that illuminated roadside vegetation receives significantly fewer visits from nocturnal pollinators. Corals, whose synchronized spawning depends on lunar cues, are confused by dock lights. Fireflies, whose entire courtship is a language of darkness, cannot speak it under sodium vapor.

Our own bodies keep the old ledger too. Deep in the brain, the pineal gland secretes melatonin—the hormone of darkness—only when light does not tell it otherwise, and the cells in our retinas that report ambient brightness to the brain are exquisitely sensitive to exactly the blue-rich wavelengths our screens and streetlamps favor. Chronic exposure to light at night disrupts circadian rhythms, and researchers have linked it to elevated risks of sleep disorders, metabolic disease, depression, and certain cancers. Night-shift workers carry this burden visibly. We are animals who spent millions of years calibrating ourselves to the planet's rotation, and we have recently decided, in evolutionary terms in a single afternoon, that the rotation is optional.

Something subtler has been lost as well: a library. Nearly every human culture wrote its deepest stories on the dark sky, because the dark sky was the one book everyone could read. Aboriginal Australians read the "Emu in the Sky," a constellation made not of stars but of the dark dust lanes themselves—a figure drawn in negative space, visible only to people intimate with darkness. Chinese poets wrote of the Silver River, the Milky Way, that separates the Weaver Girl star from the Cowherd star—Vega and Altair—lovers permitted to cross the celestial river just once a year over a bridge of magpies, which is why the seventh night of the seventh lunar month remains a festival of love. Farmers on five continents planted and harvested by the Pleiades. Sailors steered by Polaris. The sky was a calendar, a compass, a scripture, and a soap opera, all at once, and it was legible to every unaided eye on Earth. We have not translated that library so much as locked the building. Van Gogh painted *The Starry Night* in 1889 from Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, and the sky he gave us—swirling, blazing, alive—is often called visionary exaggeration. It may simply have been accurate reporting from a world that still had its darkness. After the 1994 earthquake knocked out power across Los Angeles, the Griffith Observatory reportedly fielded anxious calls from residents wondering about the strange silvery cloud that had appeared overhead. Some of them were looking at the Milky Way for the first time in their lives, and did not recognize their own galaxy.

There is a philosophical point buried in all this, and it is this: darkness is not the absence of meaning but its precondition. You cannot see stars except against the dark; the darker the sky, the deeper the universe it reveals. Keats praised the capacity to remain "in uncertainties, mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact and reason," and called it negative capability—the creative power of not knowing. Milton described hell as "darkness visible," but our inner darkness deserves better press: sleep, dreams, the slow unconscious work of consolidation and repair, the nightly descent we all make and wake from renewed. To abolish darkness is to abolish the interval in which things ripen. And there is a political dimension too, quieter but real: darkness is a form of privacy, the original one, the state of being unseen. A world saturated with light at every hour is a world without cover, without shadow to think in. The right to darkness is the right to be unobserved, unreached, unresolved—to be, for a few hours, nobody in particular.

None of this argues for returning to the tallow candle, and I would not romanticize a past whose nights were also cold, dangerous, and long. The argument is narrower and stranger: light only means something because darkness exists. A lamp in a window is a message precisely because the surrounding fields are black. We have not enriched light by multiplying it; we have impoverished it, flooding every surface until illumination communicates nothing. The remedy is not less civilization but better manners with photons—fixtures that shine down instead of up, warm spectra instead of harsh blue, timers and dimmers and the simple discipline of lighting what needs lighting and letting the rest be. Since 1988 the International Dark-Sky Association has certified places that protect their darkness; Natural Bridges National Monument in Utah became the first such park in 2007, and today dark-sky reserves from New Zealand's Aoraki Mackenzie to the deserts of Chile guard skies the way we guard watersheds—as infrastructure for the soul. These efforts succeed because the restoration is absurdly cheap. No technology need be invented. The switch already exists.

I think often about that night in the desert, and about what it would take to give that sight back. It would take almost nothing: a few degrees of restraint, a few billion bulbs angled downward, a willingness to let the edges of our towns dissolve into honest black. And it would give back something enormous—not just the Milky Way, but the older inheritance underneath it: the two-part sleep and the thoughtful hour between, the moonlit walk, the story told by firelight, the sense of living on a turning planet under an open universe rather than inside a lit room with the curtains painted on. The last great wilderness is not on the ground at all. It is overhead, it is free, and unlike every other wilderness, it can be restored overnight—literally, everywhere, by anyone—with the flick of a switch. All we have to do is decide that darkness, too, is worth keeping.

The user wants me to write freely about whatever I want for 2500 words. This is an open-ended creative writing request. I should write something substantive, interesting, and genuinely engaging. Let me think about what would make a good free-form essay.

I could write about:
- A personal-feeling essay on some topic I find fascinating
- An exploration of ideas — consciousness, time, language, cities, the ocean
- Something with a distinctive voice

Let me pick something rich. Ideas: the history of night and artificial light; the concept of "liminal spaces"; the deep sea; the invention of the color blue; memory and forgetting; the anthropology of sleep; lichens; the postal service; maps and blank spaces.

I think an essay about darkness/night — how humans have transformed night through artificial light — could be beautiful. Or an essay about the deep sea as Earth's largest habitat. Or something about silence. Or about the strange fact that we're made of dead stars — too cliché maybe.

Let me go with something like "In Praise of Darkness" or an essay on night, light pollution, and what we've lost — but also what darkness gives us. That's evocative, allows for science, history, personal reflection, philosophy. It can carry 2500 words well.

Alternatively, an essay about the sea's twilight zone, or about moss. Moss is lovely — small, overlooked, ancient. But night/darkness has more narrative arc.

Actually, let me consider writing about "the edge of the map" — terra incognita, how blank spaces on maps have vanished, and what that means psychologically. That's also great. Hmm.

Or I could do something more unusual: an essay on waiting rooms, or on the color of things before photography, or on the smell of rain (petrichor). Petrichor! The smell of rain on dry earth — its discovery, the science, why it moves us. That could be a wonderful essay but might be hard to stretch to 2500 words without padding.

Night/darkness essay structure:
1. Opening scene — experiencing true darkness somewhere remote
2. Historical relationship with night — pre-electric world, segmented sleep, moonlight culture
3. The arrival of artificial light — gas lamps, Edison, the transformation of cities
4. Light pollution today — 80% of Americans can't see the Milky Way, skyglow
5. What darkness does — melatonin, circadian rhythms, wildlife (sea turtles, birds, insects)
6. Astronomical loss — the Milky Way in cultural memory, Van Gogh's Starry Night skies
7. Philosophical turn — darkness as necessary contrast, the value of limits, inner darkness
8. Closing — a call not to eliminate darkness but to befriend it again

That can easily sustain 2500 words with good prose. Let me aim for roughly that length. I should count approximately — 2500 words is substantial. Let me write in sections with flowing prose, maybe with a few section breaks or just continuous essay. I'll write with care, vivid imagery, accurate facts where I include them (being careful not to fabricate precise statistics — I know commonly cited figures like "80% of North Americans cannot see the Milky Way" from the 2016 Falchi et al. study / "World Atlas of Artificial Night Sky Brightness," which found ~80% of the world's population lives under light-polluted skies, and about one-third of humanity cannot see the Milky Way, including 80% of North Americans). Segmented sleep: historian Roger Ekirch's work on "first sleep" and "second sleep." Melatonin suppressed by blue light. Sea turtle hatchlings disoriented by coastal lighting. Moths and insect decline linked to lights. Chicago's "Lights Out" program for bird migration. Van Gogh painted Starry Night in 1889 — gaslight era but rural Provence still dark. Paris was called "City of Light" partly due to early street lighting and its role in Enlightenment. Gas lamps appeared early 1800s; London's Pall Mall had gas lamps around 1807; Paris lit the Arc de Triomphe etc. Edison's Pearl Street Station 1882. Candlepower comparisons: a single candle vs modern LED floodlights. The Bortle scale for sky darkness. Dark-sky places: Big Bend, Aoraki/Mount Cook in New Zealand, Natural Bridges National Monument (first International Dark Sky Park, 2007). The International Dark-Sky Association founded 1988 by David Crawford and Tim Hunter.

Also cultural notes: pre-industrial people experienced moonlit nights vividly; "moonlight" as a noun for second jobs; night watchmen calling hours; curfew from French "couvre-feu" (cover fire). Star navigation. The Pleiades used in agricultural calendars worldwide. The Milky Way in mythologies — river of stars, silver river in Chinese mythology (Qixi festival), Waka poetry in Japan, Aboriginal Australian "Emu in the Sky" dark constellation. Nice detail: dark constellations — the Emu formed by dark dust lanes.

Philosophy: darkness as the condition for seeing stars; the unconscious; "darkness visible" (Milton); negative capability (Keats); the value of not-knowing; rest; the right to darkness as analog of the right to privacy — "the right to be unseen."

Ending: practical hope — shielded fixtures, warmer color temperatures, dark-sky reserves, turning off lights during migration seasons; the experience of seeing the Milky Way return after a blackout — e.g., after the 1994 LA earthquake, people reportedly called authorities puzzled by the strange sky (the Milky Way) — this anecdote is widely reported though possibly apocryphal-ish; I can present it carefully ("reportedly").

Let me draft with attention to word count. Roughly 2500 words. I'll write long paragraphs, maybe 10-14 paragraphs plus section breaks. Let me just write naturally and keep track. Average paragraph ~150-200 words means ~13-16 paragraphs. I'll use a few asterisk breaks perhaps, or headers? For a free essay, flowing prose with occasional breaks feels right. Maybe minimal formatting — it's creative writing, so prose is appropriate. Perhaps a title.

Draft:

Title: "The Country of Night" or "In Defense of Darkness" or "What We Lost When We Lit the World"

Opening: Describe standing somewhere truly dark — e.g., high desert, or the Atacama, or a lake in northern Ontario. Sensory details: the Milky Way casting faint shadows (it's said bright enough under pristine skies), the zodiacal light, airglow, satellites moving, meteors.

Then pivot: most humans no longer see this. Statistics. Then history: night before electricity — Ekirch's segmented sleep, moonlit activities, fear and community, curfews, candles expensive ("candlelight" as luxury; rushlights; tallow vs beeswax). Then gas and electric light: cities glowing, night becoming day, factories running shifts, the 24-hour city. Then consequences: astronomy, wildlife, human health. Then cultural memory: myths of the sky, Van Gogh. Then philosophical meditation: darkness as fertile, as rest, as the unknown that makes knowledge meaningful; darkness within us — sleep, dreams, the unconscious. Then hope/practical: dark-sky movement, shielded lights, the wonder of rediscovery. Close with returning to the opening scene image.

Let me be careful with facts:
- Falchi et al. 2016: more than 80% of world population lives under light-polluted skies; ~60% of Europeans and nearly 80% of North Americans cannot see the Milky Way. I'll phrase as "roughly four in five North Americans."
- Ekirch, "At Day's Close: Night in Times Past" (2005): biphasic sleep, "first sleep" and "second sleep" documented across cultures; interval of quiet wakefulness used for prayer, reflection, conversation, even visiting neighbors.
- Curfew etymology: couvre-feu, "cover fire."
- Gas lighting: London, early 19th century (Pall Mall 1807 demonstration; Westminster Bridge lit 1813ish). Paris earned "City of Light" nickname in 19th century partly for street lighting and intellectual luminosity.
- Edison: Pearl Street Station, Manhattan, September 1882.
- Melatonin: secreted by pineal gland in darkness; blue wavelengths (~460-480nm) most suppressive via ipRGCs containing melanopsin.
- Sea turtles: hatchlings instinctively move toward brighter horizon; beachfront lighting causes disorientation, deaths.
- Birds: up to a billion birds die annually in US building collisions (estimates vary; often cited ~365 million to 1 billion); lights attract and disorient migrating birds; "Lights Out" programs exist in many cities.
- Insects: moths drawn to flame — "dancing" around lights may be due to dorsal light response/navigation confusion; studies show streetlights reduce nocturnal pollination.
- 1994 Northridge earthquake LA blackout: Griffith Observatory reportedly received calls asking about the strange sky; some accounts say people were alarmed by the Milky Way. Widely reported anecdote; I'll hedge slightly.
- Natural Bridges National Monument: first certified International Dark-Sky Park (2007).
- IDA founded 1988.
- Bortle scale: Class 1 pristine to Class 9 inner-city.
- Airglow: faint natural glow of atmosphere; even darkest sites aren't perfectly black.
- Zodiacal light: sunlight scattered by interplanetary dust, visible as false dawn.
- Venus/moonlight shadows: full moon bright enough to cast shadows; under very dark skies the Milky Way itself is sometimes said to cast faint shadows (reported by observers at pristine sites).
- Aboriginal "Emu in the Sky": dark constellation in Coalsack region near Southern Cross.
- Chinese mythology: Silver River (Milky Way) separating Weaver Girl and Cowherd stars (Vega and Altair), Qixi festival, magpie bridge once a year.
- Milton: "darkness visible" from Paradise Lost describing Hell.
- Keats: negative capability — "capable of being in uncertainties, Mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact & reason."
- Van Gogh, Starry Night, June 1889, Saint-Rémy-de-Provence; Venus actually depicted (morning star) per letters; painted from memory/imagination blended with observation.
